subject: Culture
title: How English Won
description: A fast breakdown of How English Won for builders.

hook.text: 75% of the world's scientific papers are in English. A Japanese physicist must publish in English or be invisible.

buildup.text: English piggy-backed on the British Empire, then American economic and cultural dominance after 1945.

discovery.text: It wasn't quality that won. French was the diplomatic language for centuries. Latin ruled science until the 1700s.

twist.text: Most English speakers today are non-native. They're reshaping the language faster than native speakers can.

climax.text: Singlish, Hinglish, and other hybrids may evolve into separate languages within a few generations.

punchline.text: English won by accident, and its winners keep changing it.

quiz.question: What percentage of scientific papers are in English?

details.summary: English's global dominance is not natural — it was manufactured through British colonialism, American economic power, and Hollywood's cultural reach. English is the language of aviation, science, finance, and the internet not because it is linguistically superior but because its speakers held power.
details.whyItMatters: English's dominance shapes who has access to global opportunities. Understanding it as historical accident, not linguistic merit, challenges the assumption that English is the 'natural' global language.
takeaways: English is the official language in over 50 countries
About 1.5 billion people speak English worldwide, most as a second language
English dominates science: over 95% of scientific papers are in English

faq.question: Why did English become the global language?
faq.answer: Three overlapping waves: British colonialism (17th-20th centuries) spread English across five continents. American economic and military dominance (20th century) made English the language of commerce, science, and diplomacy.

faq.question: Is English linguistically superior to other languages?
faq.answer: No. Linguists unanimously agree that no language is inherently superior. English has a large vocabulary (drawing from Germanic and Romance roots) but chaotic spelling, no formal-informal pronoun distinction, and relatively simple grammar.
